title: Hazratbal Crisis and Communal Tensions in East Pakistan
subtitle: The Hazratbal relic theft and communal violence in East Pakistan, 1963–1964
summary: The Indian Commission of Jurists' Committee of Enquiry framed the Hazratbal relic theft as the immediate context for migration from East Pakistan in 1964. Its report says the relic was reported missing on 27 December 1963 and found on 4 January 1964; it dates disturbances in Khulna to 3 January. The committee attributed the crisis to rhetoric and meetings held after the relic episode, and its Khulna account describes a procession, violence and later official and military responses. These are the committee's interpretations and reports, based on evidence from migrants and others on the Indian side; it says Pakistan did not reply to its request to visit East Pakistan.
heroTagline: A committee inquiry into the Hazratbal relic episode and East Pakistan in 1963–64
whyItMatters: The 1965 inquiry links a Kashmir shrine episode with reported communal tensions and migration in East Pakistan, and presents a causal account centered on public rhetoric and meetings after the relic episode. Its preface also makes the limits of its evidence clear: the committee gathered testimony in India and says Pakistan did not answer its request to visit East Pakistan. Those limits matter when reading its interpretation of causes and its description of responses as the committee's account rather than neutral findings.

claimCitations.claim: The committee dates the relic's reported disappearance to 27 December 1963 and its recovery to 4 January 1964, dates the Khulna disturbances to 3 January, and attributes a connection to the relic episode; these are the committee's claims.
The committee says it gathered testimony from migrants and others in India and received no acknowledgement or reply to its request to visit East Pakistan.

The committee's account describes post-relic rhetoric and meetings, a procession in Khulna, violence, official statements, and the army being called in; its account draws on migrants and others interviewed in India.

contentWarnings: Communal violence and religious-site desecration claims
